The central question is: under what conditions does the fusion plan produced at compile time remain valid at runtime, given that mixed-precision scheduling (e.g., BF16 accumulation inside a fused op that expects FP32 inputs from an upstream cast) and dynamic shapes (batch size or sequence length unknown until inference) can silently invalidate the assumptions the compiler baked in. Beginners think of fusion as a pure optimization — if it works once, it works. Experts worry about recompilation triggers: a dynamic shape that falls outside the profiled bucket causes a cache miss, the runtime falls back to an unfused eager path, and now your precision contract is different because the un-fused ops each round independently, producing subtly different outputs than the fused kernel would have. The deeper anxiety is operator scheduling interleaving: when a mixed-precision graph has both fused and unfused subgraphs executing concurrently across CUDA streams, intermediate tensor dtypes can diverge from what the fusion boundary assumed, and the resulting numerical error is not an exception — it's a silent wrong answer that only surfaces in loss curves or output distributions, not in any runtime check.

The fundamental issue is that KV cache reuse and speculative decoding make the serving lane non-Markovian with respect to individual requests: the numerical path for request N depends on which KV blocks were populated by requests 1 through N-1, so two lanes processing the same current request but with different cache histories will diverge even with identical kernels and hardware, making naive lane comparison useless as a numerical regression signal. The correct abstraction is to shift comparison from request-level to session-level with cache state synchronization: you define a counterfactual lane as one that receives an identical cache state snapshot at session start, processes the same request sequence, and is compared at session boundaries rather than per-request — TensorRT-LLM's paged KV cache design makes this tractable because cache blocks are content-addressed, so you can fork a cache state to both lanes by copying block pointers rather than tensor data, adding ~microseconds of overhead rather than duplicating gigabytes of KV tensors. Speculative decoding adds a second layer of state dependence because the draft model's accepted token sequence changes which KV positions are populated, creating path-dependent cache layouts that diverge between lanes even from identical inputs if the draft acceptance rates differ by even one token — the mitigation is to run speculative decoding in deterministic replay mode on the counterfactual lane, forcing it to accept exactly the tokens the primary lane accepted rather than re-running the draft, which isolates the numerical comparison to the verify kernel rather than the full speculative path.
